## Task 1, lets break down the following boxplots

This creates a single boxplot for the variable p2sales from the store.df data frame.

This boxplot represents the weekly sales (p2sales) for all stores combined, without distinguishing between different stores.
For a more comprehensive analysis, you need to break down the data by meaningful categories, such as by store.

xlab = "Weekly sales": Label for the x-axis, representing the weekly sales values.
ylab = "P2": Label for the y-axis, which can be used to indicate the product or item being analyzed (in this case, "P2").
main = "Weekly sales of P2, All stores": The title of the boxplot.
horizontal = TRUE: The boxplot is drawn horizontally, with the x-axis showing the sales values and the y-axis indicating "P2".

```{r}
boxplot(store.df$p2sales, xlab="Weekly sales", ylab="P2",
        main="Weekly sales of P2, All stores", horizontal=TRUE)
```

This code creates multiple boxplots, one for each store in the dataset (storeNum).The ~ operator is used here to create boxplots for p2sales by store. Each boxplot represents the distribution of weekly sales (p2sales) for a different store.In R, the ~ can be read as "by", meaning the boxplots will be grouped based on the unique values of storeNum.

Each unique storeNum will generate a separate boxplot. 

ylab = "Store": Labels the y-axis, indicating that each boxplot corresponds to a different store.
xlab = "Weekly unit sales": Labels the x-axis, which shows the sales data.
las = 1: Rotates the y-axis labels to be horizontal, making the store labels easier to read.
main = "Weekly Sales of P2 by Store": The title of the plot.
horizontal = TRUE: The boxplots are horizontal, with sales values on the x-axis.
 
```{r}
boxplot(store.df$p2sales ~ store.df$storeNum, horizontal=TRUE,
        ylab="Store", xlab="Weekly unit sales", las=1,
        main="Weekly Sales of P2 by Store")
```

## Task 2:  Discuss the use of [ ] brackets which contain conditional row and column expressions in R.

This line of R code creates a histogram for the mpce variable in the df5 data frame, but only for the values of mpce that are less than 30,000.

hist(df5$mpce[df5$mpce<30000])

df5$mpce: This selects the mpce column from the data frame df5
df5$mpce < 30000: This condition checks which values in the mpce column are less than 30,000. It returns a vector of TRUE or FALSE values.
df5$mpce[df5$mpce < 30000]: This subsetting operation uses the condition to extract only the values of mpce that satisfy the condition (i.e., mpce values less than 30,000).
hist(): The hist() function creates a histogram of the filtered values. 

The expression df5$mpce[df5$mpce < 30000] only focuses on filtering rows based on a condition for one specific column, which is mpce. 


## Task 3: Construct a histogram

This command is creating a histogram of the store.spend column in the cust.df data frame.

The breaks argument controls how the data is divided into bins (intervals) in the histogram.
max(cust.df$store.spend) calculates the maximum value of the store.spend column.
ceiling(max(cust.df$store.spend)/10) rounds up this maximum value to the nearest 10.
0:ceiling(...) creates a sequence of numbers from 0 to this rounded maximum.
Multiplying by 10 ensures that the bin width is set to 10

```{r}
cust.df <- read.csv("http://goo.gl/PmPkaG")
```

```{r}
hist(cust.df$store.spend, 
     breaks=(0:ceiling(max(cust.df$store.spend)/10))*10,
     main="Customers as of June 2014", 
     xlab="Prior 12 months in-store sales ($)", 
     ylab="Count of customers")
```

## Task 4:Create a kernel density diagram

d <- density(store.df$p2prom):
density() generates a kernel density estimate.
store.df$p2prom is referring to a column named p2prom in the dataframe store.df.
The result is stored in d, containing the estimated density data.
plot(d):
This plots the density estimate stored in d. 

```{r}
d <- density(store.df$p2prom)
plot(d)
```
